query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The oxidation resistance of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) at elevated temperatures is due to a synergy between high configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion that enables the selective oxidation of minor, protective elements (e.g., Al or Cr) to form a dense, adherent mixed-oxide layer that self-limits further oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, equiatomic (or near-equiatomic) high-entropy alloy (for example, an AlCoCrFeNi or CrTa-based HEA) with a single-phase or minimally segregated microstructure.
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA sample to a high-temperature oxidizing environment (e.g., 800–1100 °C in air) for a controlled period.
generation.conditions: Keep temperature, oxygen partial pressure, and exposure time constant; perform a controlled comparison between the HEA and a conventional alloy with similar constituent elements but lower configurational entropy.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a protective oxide film that is enriched in selectively oxidized elements (e.g., a thin, continuous layer of Al2O3 or Cr-rich oxides) at the alloy’s surface.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy in HEAs promotes sluggish diffusion of alloying elements. This limited mobility allows for the controlled, preferential oxidation of elements with strong oxide-forming tendencies, resulting in a uniform, well-adherent oxide scale. The mixed nature of this oxide, stabilized by the presence of several elements, resists further oxygen ingress and prevents the formation of non-protective, rapidly growing oxide phases.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional alloys, HEAs will develop a thinner, more uniform, and adherent oxide layer that grows at a slower rate, as evidenced by reduced mass gains and more favorable oxide phase compositions under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: The oxidation behavior observed in conventional alloys with similar primary elements but lower configurational entropy, which typically develop thicker and less protective oxide scales.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be effective only in HEA systems that include elements capable of forming stable, protective oxides. Systems lacking such elements or where volatile oxides dominate may not follow this behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The precise balance between the effect of sluggish diffusion and the selective oxidation of protective elements remains to be quantified, and the composition and structure of the oxide scale may vary with specific alloy chemistries and environmental conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy systems: (1) a high-entropy alloy designed with protective oxide-forming elements (e.g., Cr and Al) and (2) a conventional alloy with a similar nominal composition but lower configurational entropy. Subject both samples to high-temperature oxidation (e.g., at 900 °C in air) under identical conditions. Characterize the oxide scale’s thickness, morphology, phase composition, and adhesion over time using thermogravimetric analysis, X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, and adhesion tests.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and uniformity (via cross-sectional SEM)
Phase composition of the oxide scale (XRD/XPS)
Adhesion strength of the oxide layer (mechanical testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy does not show a significantly slower oxidation rate, a thinner and more uniform protective oxide layer (e.g., enriched in Al2O3 or Cr-oxides), or improved oxide adhesion compared to the conventional alloy, then the proposed mechanism of high configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion promoting selective, protective oxidation is refuted.

Thermodynamic Insights into the Oxidation Mechanisms of CrMnFeCoNi High-Entropy Alloy Using In Situ X-ray Diffraction

Abstract: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr2O3, Fe2O3, or Fe3O4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Initial Oxidation Behavior of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Coating Produced by Atmospheric Plasma Spraying in the Range of 650 °C to 1000 °C

Abstract: AbstractAs protective coatings for the thermal parts of aero-engines, AlCoCrFeNi coatings have good application prospects. In this study, atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) was used to prepare AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy coatings (HECs), which were oxidized from 650 °C to 1000 °C. The mechanism of the oxide layer formation and the internal phase transition were systematically investigated. The results show that a mixed oxide scale with a laminated structure was formed at the initial stage of oxidation. The redistribution of elements and phase transition occurred in the HECs’ matrix; the BCC/B2 structure transformed to Al-Ni ordered B2 phase and Fe-Cr disordered A2 phase.Keywords: plasma spraying, oxidation behavior, high-entropy coatings, phase transition

Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys

Abstract: Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions. An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide

Abstract: AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours.
